extracted.intended_audience: general readers interested in finance, short-selling, and corporate investigative reports
extracted.subtask_description: Practices and operating procedures used by an activist short-selling firm to prepare and publish investigative reports alleging corporate fraud, and the related trading/distribution behavior. The page documents methods, disclosure choices, and public/post-publication interactions with targets and regulators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigation methodology
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepared investigation reports on target companies by going through their public records, internal corporate documents and by talking to employees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This describes the core research steps Hindenburg used: review public filings/records, examine internal documents, and conduct employee interviews. Examples on the page include reports on Nikola, Tingo, Super Micro, etc., where documentary evidence and interviews were central to the allegations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-release distribution and trading coordination
rubrics_metrics.description: Each report was then circulated to Hindenburg's limited partners, who, together with Hindenburg, took out a short position in the target company before publicly releasing the report.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The firm coordinated short positions with limited partners prior to the public release of a report. The page notes this as the operational model and explains Hindenburg profited if the target company's share price declined after publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allegation focus — fraud, debt, and accounting concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Reports allege corporate fraud and malfeasance, flag debt and accounting concerns, and identify alleged misrepresentations (e.g., founder credentials, partner relationships).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple reports (Adani, Nikola, Tingo, Supermicro, etc.) centered on claims of misrepresented financials, debt/accounting issues, and factual misstatements. Outcomes cited include share-price declines, regulatory inquiries (SEC, DOJ), and litigation or scrutiny. The page uses these examples as evidence of the firm's focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public justification and defense of short-selling
rubrics_metrics.description: The reports also featured defenses of the practice of short-selling and explanations of how short-sells 'play a critical role in exposing fraud and protecting investors.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hindenburg's publications included normative material explaining why short-selling is valuable and legitimate. This suggests reports are framed not only as exposés but also as public-interest arguments about market oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure practices regarding positions
rubrics_metrics.description: Hindenburg sometimes disclosed whether it held short or long positions in a subject (e.g., disclosed it had no short/long positions in Clover Health; disclosed short positions in Adani).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page documents that disclosure practices varied by report. In Clover Health Hindenburg disclosed no positions; in other cases (Adani, Super Micro, etc.) it disclosed short positions. This implies a criterion around whether and how to disclose trading positions when publishing an investigative report.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of provocative / adversarial public tactics
rubrics_metrics.description: Hindenburg called on targets to sue if they believed a report was inaccurate and publicly dared companies (e.g., Adani) to take legal action, often standing by their statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page records that Hindenburg publicly challenged targets to sue and publicly defended its work when met with accusations, indicating an adversarial public posture as part of its publication strategy. Examples: daring Adani to sue; releasing follow-up statements when challenged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sourcing incentives and bounties
rubrics_metrics.description: Hindenburg announced monetary rewards (a $1 million reward) for information relevant to certain investigations (e.g., on Tether's reserves).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The firm at times offered bounties to incentivize whistleblowers or sources to provide information. The page cites the October 2021 $1M reward as an example of using financial incentives to gather evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation of regulatory and legal consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Reports often led to regulatory inquiries, legal responses, or reputational/market consequences (e.g., SEC inquiries, DOJ probes, auditor resignations, stock price drops, show-cause notices from SEBI).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page repeatedly documents downstream effects (SEC inquiries after Nikola; SEBI showcause after Adani; DOJ probes after Supermicro; auditor resignations). This functions as implicit guidance that thorough documentation and legal preparedness are important when publishing such allegations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification of third-party claims (credentials, partnerships, contracts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reports questioned legitimacy of claimed partnerships, founder credentials, and business relationships (e.g., alleged misrepresentation of founder's educational credentials and claimed partners for Tingo Group).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hindenburg's approach included fact-checking and verification (or allegation of misrepresentation) of third-party claims such as academic credentials and partner relationships. The page shows these checks as recurring content elements of their reports.
